That’s a really good way to start—one clear, meaningful project, and just enough setup to support it. You don’t need to turn the garage into a full workshop overnight.

For a first pass, think “simple, straight, and sturdy,” not fine furniture. You can absolutely work up to cherry later, but for learning, it’s better to use something forgiving and affordable. Pine or “select” boards from a home improvement store are ideal to start with. They’re softer, easier to cut, and if you make a mistake, it won’t feel like you’ve ruined something precious. Once you’ve got a feel for it, you could build the “real” version in cherry.

On tools, you can keep this surprisingly minimal:

- A circular saw (for cutting boards to size)  
- A drill/driver (for making holes and driving screws)  
- A measuring tape and a good square (this matters more than people expect)  
- Clamps (at least a couple—these act like an extra set of hands)  
- Sandpaper or a simple electric sander  

That’s enough to build a solid set of shelves. You don’t need a table saw or anything elaborate yet.

You’ll also want a basic work surface. It doesn’t have to be fancy—a pair of sawhorses with a sheet of plywood across them works perfectly well to start.

For the design, keep it straightforward: two vertical sides, a top, a bottom, and a few fixed shelves in between. Rectangular, no curves, no complicated joinery. You can use screws and wood glue—strong, reliable, and beginner-friendly. The key is measuring carefully and keeping everything square as you assemble.

One practical tip that saves frustration: have the store cut the larger boards down for you. Most places will do a few cuts for free or very cheap, and it makes handling everything much easier in a small space.

As for the space you described—twelve by twenty with power and lighting—that’s more than enough. You’ll be comfortable in there.

And here’s something worth saying plainly: don’t aim for perfection on this first one. Aim for “solid and finished.” You’ll learn more from completing a slightly imperfect bookshelf than from planning a flawless one that never quite gets built.

If you’d like, we can sketch out rough dimensions for the shelves based on your living room and what Margaret had in mind—height, width, how many shelves, that sort of thing—and turn this into a very concrete first build.
